Mihai is (once again) an hour late for dinner. Ana is upset.
At last! I’ve been waiting for an hour. Why didn’t you call me?
I’m really sorry. There was an emergency at the hospital and my battery died.
It’s not the first time, Mihai. It really bothers me to wait without knowing anything.
And it worries me: you work too much. You never have time for anything.
You’re right. It gets on my nerves too. I’m fed up with so many night shifts.
And don’t you care that we spend so little time together?
Of course I care! It makes me really sad. When I’m at the hospital, I miss you.
Really. Look, what do you think of this idea? Next month I’ll ask for fewer shifts.
I think that’s a very good idea. And one more thing: buy yourself a power bank.
Ha, ha. Deal. Do you forgive me?
I forgive you… but only because I’m very interested in the dinner you’re taking me to tomorrow.
Tomorrow? Oops! I’m on call tomorrow…

Spaniards express their emotions with strong intonation: “¡Por fin!” (irritation), “¿De verdad?” (hope), “¡Mihai!” (amused reproach). Copy the tone, not just the words.
1. The GUSTAR family: verbs of feeling
Many verbs of feeling work exactly like GUSTAR (chapter 11): the thing is the subject and the person is “to me, to you…”. Literally “the noise bothers TO ME”.
I don’t care. / It doesn’t matter.
The rule is the same: one thing / an infinitive → singular verb (me molesta); several things → plural (me molestan los ruidos).
For emotions that come as a reaction, Spanish uses “me pone + adjective”. The adjective agrees with the PERSON:
Traffic gets on my nerves. (a man)
Seeing my friends puts me in a good mood.
A woman says “me pone nerviosA”. The adjective shows who feels it, not what causes it.
Me da vergüenza hablar en público.
I’m embarrassed to speak in public.
I feel sorry for that dog.
I don’t mind. / I don’t care.
An alternative with TENER: Tengo miedo de los perros (I’m afraid of dogs). Tengo vergüenza.
PARECER also works like GUSTAR and is the most elegant way to ask for or give an opinion:
What do you think of the plan?
I think it’s brilliant / fine / terrible.
I think it’s going to rain.
The prices seem high to me.
I love you. (both; “te amo” is more intense)
“Echar de menos” is the expression used in Spain. In Latin America people say “Te extraño”.
I’m fed up with the rain.
I think that’s a very good idea.

La carta que Ana nunca envió
While tidying her desk, Ana found a letter she had written a year and a half earlier, a few months after meeting Mihai. She had never given it to him.
She opened it and started to read, a little embarrassed.
“Dear Mihai: I’m writing to you because I’m too embarrassed to tell you these things face to face. I get very nervous when I’m with you.”
“I love the way you laugh when you don’t understand a word in Spanish. Your accent makes me smile, and I find it lovely that you always ask about my grandmother.”
“But there are also things that worry me. I’m afraid of falling in love with someone who might go back to Romania one day.”
“It makes me sad to think that your family is so far away and that you miss them. And I have to admit it bothers me a little that you work so many hours.”
“I don’t know what you feel. Maybe for you I’m just a friend, the teacher who teaches you new words on Sundays.”
“If that’s the case, it’s fine. I care about you a lot and I want you to be happy, even if it’s not with me.”
“But if you feel the same as me… call me. I’ll be waiting. Ana.”
Ana left the letter on the table and smiled. She remembered that time perfectly: the doubts, the nerves, the sleepless nights thinking about him.
In the end she didn’t need the letter. A week later Mihai asked her out to dinner and told her, in terrible Spanish, that he had fallen in love with her.
At that moment Mihai came into the room. “What’s that?”, he asked. Ana hesitated for a second. Then she gave him the letter.
Mihai read it in silence. When he finished, his eyes were a little wet.
“You’re a year and a half late,” he said with a smile. “But I’m glad you didn’t give it to me back then. That way I got to say it first.”
Ana put the letter in a box, next to the photo of their first coffee in the square. Some letters don’t need to be sent.
That same evening Mihai wrote his own letter. He didn’t give it to Ana: he put it in the same box, under hers.
On the envelope he wrote: “To be read on our wedding day”.
Mihai never told Ana what he had written. She never asked him either. Some secrets can wait.

Text to read: The making-up message
Mihai writes to Ana the next day.
Ana, yesterday I felt terrible. I’m so sorry I made you wait.
I’ve spoken to my boss and next month I’ll only have four night shifts.
And I’ve swapped tomorrow’s shift with a colleague.
So tomorrow at nine I’m taking you out to dinner. What do you say? I love you.
